problem: The pipeline shown runs World → Window → Norm → Viewport → Device and never mentions clipping, although clipping is one of the standard stages of the 2D viewing pipeline (it normally happens in normalized or window coordinates, before the viewport map). A student reading only the figure will think the pipeline has no clipping stage.
fix: Add a clipping node between the window/normalizing stage and the viewport, and say in Section 1 that the scene is clipped against the window (normally after normalization and before the viewport map) and that the details are in 2.6.

where: Section 1, Normalized coordinates bullet, against the Beyond paragraph
problem: Section 1 says normalized coordinates run from 0 to 1, while the Beyond paragraph says GPUs take normalized device coordinates in the range −1 to 1. Both conventions exist, but as written the two statements look contradictory to a student.
fix: State that two conventions are in use: 0 to 1 in the classical pipeline, and −1 to 1 in OpenGL/Vulkan normalized device coordinates; the scale-and-shift is the same, only the numbers change.

problem: The answer says the last column holds the shift and gives (100, 60, 1) for a viewport starting at (100, 60). That value is only correct because the window starts at the origin; a student will generalise the last column to (xvmin, yvmin, 1), which is wrong when xwmin or ywmin is not zero.
fix: Give the general form: the last column is (xvmin − xwmin·sx, yvmin − ywmin·sy, 1), which reduces to (100, 60, 1) here only because xwmin = ywmin = 0.

problem: The sentence 'so a viewport placed in the corner of the screen puts the picture in the wrong place' does not support the trap: if the viewport start is (0, 0), dropping xvmin changes nothing. The intended case is a viewport that does not start at the origin.
fix: Rewrite: dropping xvmin always draws the picture as if the viewport started at the origin, so when the viewport is offset from the origin the picture appears at the wrong place on the screen.

problem: The world point (5, 5) is the window's top-right corner and maps to (400, 400), the outer boundary of a viewport declared as (0, 0) to (400, 400). If that viewport is 400 pixels wide, its inside pixels are numbered 0 to 399, so (400, 400) lies just past the last pixel; a student may be unsure whether the corner pixel is drawn.
fix: Add one line: viewport edges are treated as continuous boundaries, so a point exactly on xwmax maps to the edge value xvmax = 400, which is the boundary of the 400-pixel-wide region; interior scene points land between 0 and 400 and their pixels are 0 to 399.
